title: Linux syscall tables across 27 architectures
excerpt: A site now lists every Linux syscall number, arguments and registers for 27 architectures from kernel 3.3 to 7.3.
body:
Linux 5.19 added a brand-new architecture, LoongArch, and the kernel now ships with 323 system calls for it. At the same time, the i386 table still lists 441 calls that have been stable since Linux 3.3. Getting the exact number, argument registers and entry instruction for any of those calls used to mean digging through several kernel trees, hunting down `SYSCALL_DEFINE` macros, or piecing together scattered documentation.  

The updated syscall.sh site puts every syscall table for 27 architectures in one place, covering every mainline release from Linux 3.3 to 7.3. The result is a single, authoritative source that can be browsed, downloaded as JSON, or queried through an HTTP API.  

Below are the main things the site provides, how the JSON files are structured, and how the API can be used to automate compatibility checks.

## Architecture coverage in concrete numbers  

The collection spans the most common desktop, server and embedded targets, plus a few research-oriented CPUs. Each architecture page lists the total syscall count, the kernel release where the table starts, and the ABI used for argument passing.  

* x86-64 (x64), 439 syscalls, since 3.3  
* i386 (32-bit x86), 441 syscalls, since 3.3  
* ARM EABI (32-bit), 426 syscalls, since 4.10  
* RISC-V 64, 327 syscalls, since 4.15  
* LoongArch 64, 323 syscalls, since 5.19  

Older 32-bit families such as m68k (435 calls) and arc (350 calls) are still present, and niche targets like hexagon (345 calls) or xtensa (388 calls) are included as well. Every entry shows the syscall number (`NR`), up to six argument registers (`ARG0`-`ARG5`), and the instruction that transfers control to the kernel (for example `syscall` on x86-64 or `ecall` on RISC-V). Short descriptions come from the Linux man-pages project, while `io_uring` entries are sourced from liburing.

## JSON files capture the full history  

Each architecture has a plain JSON file at `/<arch>/syscalls.json`. The file records every syscall that ever existed for that ABI, together with the kernel release where it first appeared (`since`) and, if applicable, the release where it was removed (`removed_in`). Because the generator walks every `SYSCALL_DEFINE` macro in every mainline release, the JSON reflects exactly what the kernel dispatches.

A typical record looks like this:

```json
{
  "nr": 0,
  "name": "read",
  "since": "3.3",
  "removed_in": null,
  "args": ["ARG0", "ARG1", "ARG2"],
  "return": "RETURN",
  "instruction": "syscall"
}
```

The fields map directly to the kernel’s view: `nr` is the numeric identifier, `name` the symbolic name, `since` the first release that exported the call, `removed_in` the release that dropped it (or `null` if still present), `args` the registers that hold the arguments, `return` the register that receives the result, and `instruction` the assembly opcode that triggers the transition to kernel mode.

The site’s kernel selector lets users view “all, with removed” entries, so even deprecated calls stay visible with a clear drop-point label. This historical view is useful when maintaining legacy code that still references a syscall removed in, say, Linux 5.0.

## Using the versioned API  

Static JSON downloads are handy, but many workflows need programmatic access to a specific kernel version or a diff between two releases. The site provides a REST-style API at `https://api.syscall.sh/v2/`. Requests follow the pattern:

```
https://api.syscall.sh/v2/syscalls/<arch>/<name>?kernel=<release>
```

For example, to fetch the current definition of `read` on the x64 ABI:

```
curl https://api.syscall.sh/v2/syscalls/x64/read
```

The response returns the same fields as the JSON file, plus the exact kernel version that introduced the entry.  

Diff queries compare two releases and list added or removed syscalls:

```
https://api.syscall.sh/v2/diff/x64?from=5.0&to=5.10
```

The response is a short JSON object with `added` and `removed` arrays, each containing syscall names and numbers. This makes it trivial to script compatibility checks, generate version-specific header files, or alert a build system when a required call disappears in a newer kernel.

## How the data stays accurate  

All data on syscall.sh is generated directly from the kernel source tree. For each architecture, the generator parses the syscall table and every `SYSCALL_DEFINE` macro across all mainline releases it scans. It records the calling convention (which registers hold arguments), the entry instruction, and the short description from the man-pages project. When a new kernel release is added, the site is rebuilt automatically, ensuring that the numbers match exactly what the kernel actually dispatches.

The generator also notes when a syscall disappears. Rather than deleting the entry, it adds a `removed_in` tag, preserving the historical record. This mirrors the kernel’s own treatment of deprecated syscalls, which remain in the source for documentation but are no longer reachable at runtime.

## The takeaway  

syscall.sh now centralizes every Linux syscall table for 27 architectures, complete with per-call history and a versioned API. The JSON files record when each call entered and left the kernel, and the API lets scripts fetch a single release or compare two releases without digging through source trees. Use the site or API to verify syscall numbers, argument registers, or to track changes across kernel versions, and eliminate the need to hunt through scattered kernel headers.
